chapters.title: Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

terms.def: The rate at which velocity changes, in m/s². An object accelerates when its speed changes, its direction changes, or both.
The acceleration of a system's center of mass, a_sys = ΣF_ext / m_sys: the net external force divided by the total mass. Internal forces do not enter.
A graph of acceleration a against time t. The area between it and the time axis is the change in velocity.
The object that exerts a force. A free-body diagram label names the type and the agent: "F_N, floor on box".
The largest displacement from the equilibrium position during an oscillation, A; half the distance between the turning points.
The rate of change of angular velocity, α = Δω/Δt, in rad/s². When α and ω have the same sign the object speeds up; opposite signs, it slows.
The change in an object’s angle, Δθ = θ − θ₀, in radians, with a sign for the direction of turning (counterclockwise positive is a common choice).
A torque times the time it acts, τΔt (the area under a torque-time graph), in N·m·s. It equals the change in angular momentum: τΔt = ΔL.
The rotational partner of momentum. For a rigid object turning about a fixed axis, L = Iω, in kg·m²/s; its sign gives the direction of turning.

terms.term: angular momentum of a point object
terms.def: For a point object moving past a chosen point, L = rmv sin θ: its momentum times the perpendicular distance from the point to its line of motion. It depends on the point chosen.
The rate of change of angle, ω = Δθ/Δt, in rad/s. Its sign says whether the object turns clockwise or counterclockwise.

The force a scale or floor pushes up with: the normal force. It equals mg only when the object's acceleration is zero; it is larger when accelerating up, smaller when accelerating down, and zero in free fall (weightlessness).
The distance traveled along a circle of radius r while turning through an angle θ in radians: s = rθ.
The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid the object displaces: F_b = ρ_fluid V_displaced g. It does not depend on the object's own density.
The area between a graph and the horizontal axis over an interval. Its unit is (y unit) × (x unit); area below the axis counts as negative.
Change in velocity divided by the time interval: a(avg) = Δv/Δt, in m/s². It points the same way as Δv.
Displacement divided by the time interval: v(avg) = Δx/Δt, in m/s. Its sign gives the direction of the net change in position.
The labels on a graph's axes: the quantity and its unit, such as "Time (s)". The independent variable (the one you choose or control) usually goes on the horizontal axis.
The line about which an object turns. Every point of the object moves in a circle centered on this line.

A curve whose road is tilted toward the center. On a frictionless banked curve the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal net force, at one speed: tan θ = v²/(gr). Curves that need friction are treated in words only.
P₁ + ρgy₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ρgy₂ + ½ρv₂² along an ideal fluid's flow: conservation of energy per unit volume.
A straight line drawn through scattered data with about as many points above it as below. It is never drawn dot to dot; its slope uses all the data.
The net upward force a fluid exerts on an object in it, because the pressure on the object's bottom is larger than on its top.
The mass-weighted average position of a system: x_cm = Σmᵢxᵢ ÷ Σmᵢ (the same for y). It lies on any line of symmetry of a uniform object, and the system moves as if all its mass were there.
The acceleration of an object moving in a circle, pointing toward the center, of size a_c = v²/r.

The net force toward the center of a circular path, of size mv²/r. It is not a separate force: one or more real forces (tension, friction, normal force, gravity) supply it, and it is never drawn as its own arrow on a free-body diagram.
When a system changes shape with no net external torque (a skater pulling in her arms), its rotational inertia changes and its angular velocity changes the opposite way so that L = Iω stays the same.
Deciding which objects are inside the system; it determines which forces are internal (cannot change the total momentum) and which are external (can).
The circular path of a satellite or moon around a central body, with gravity supplying the centripetal net force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r), independent of the satellite's own mass.
A system that no energy enters or leaves: no external force does net work on it. An open system exchanges energy with its surroundings.
A number with no unit, μ, that describes how strongly two particular surfaces grip: friction = μ × normal force (the maximum, for static friction). It depends on the materials, not on area or speed.
The model of a brief, strong interaction (a collision or an explosion) in which internal forces far exceed external ones, so the system's momentum is the same just before and just after.
A mass on a string swinging in a horizontal circle so that the string traces a cone. The vertical part of the tension balances the weight, and the horizontal part supplies the centripetal net force.
Objects joined by ideal strings or pushing on each other so that they share one acceleration, such as a cart pulled by a hanging block or an Atwood machine (two masses hung over one pulley).
The total angular momentum of a system stays constant when the net external torque on it is zero. The parts can trade angular momentum, but the total does not change.
Energy is never created or destroyed: a system's energy changes only by the energy transferred across its boundary.
When the net external force on a system is zero, the system's total momentum stays constant.
A force whose work depends only on the start and end positions (gravity, an ideal spring). A force whose work depends on the path, like kinetic friction, is nonconservative.
Motion in which the velocity changes by the same amount in every equal time interval: a straight, sloped v-t graph and a horizontal a-t graph.
A force between objects that touch: the normal force, tension and friction. At the scale of atoms these are electric forces between the surfaces.
For an incompressible fluid in a full pipe, the volume flow rate is the same everywhere: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. It expresses conservation of mass.
The choice of an origin (zero point) and a positive direction (an x-axis) used to give positions as numbers.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: The calculator setting that reads angles in degrees. Physics 1 angles are in degrees; in any other mode, sin and cos of a degree value come out wrong.
The Greek letter Δ (delta) in front of a symbol means "change in": final value minus initial value. Δx = x − x₀.
Mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V, in kg/m³. A property of the material, not of the amount; water is about 1000 kg/m³.
y is directly proportional to x (y ∝ x) when y = kx for a constant k: multiplying x by any factor multiplies y by the same factor.
The change in position: final position minus starting position. A vector; along a line its sign gives its direction.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: The total length of the path an object travels: a scalar that counts every meter and never decreases.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the system is the same before and after (momentum is also conserved).
The potential energy stored in a stretched or compressed ideal spring: U_s = ½k(Δx)², with Δx measured from the relaxed length.

An oval orbit with the central body off center. The satellite moves fastest at its closest point and slowest at its farthest; the total energy and the angular momentum about the central body stay constant while K and U trade.
A scalar quantity a system has that can change form and move between objects; measured in joules.
Bars showing each form of a system's energy at two moments, plus any work across the boundary; the bars must balance.

terms.term: energy of a simple harmonic oscillator
terms.def: The total mechanical energy of an oscillating system, constant with no friction; for a block on a spring it equals ½kA², shared between kinetic and spring potential energy.
Energy moving into or out of a system across its boundary, for example by work done by an external force.
The position where the net force on an oscillating object is zero; the center of its oscillation.
The smallest speed that lets an object reach infinite separation from a body: the speed at which the total energy is zero, v = √(2GM/r).
A force exerted on a system by an object outside it. Only external forces can change how the system's center of mass moves.
A substance that flows and takes the shape of its container, because its particles can move past one another: a liquid or a gas.
A small, imagined portion of a fluid treated as an object, so Newton's laws can be applied to it.
A push or pull exerted on an object by another object, with a size and a direction (a vector). Unit: the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
A force between objects that do not touch. In this course the only one is gravity, such as Earth's pull on a falling ball.
A diagram of an extended object that draws each force from the point where it acts, labeled with its type and agent, so torques about an axis can be read from it.
A graph of the force along the motion against position; the area under it is the work done by the force.
A graph of force against time; the area under it is the impulse.
Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance negligible. Near Earth every freely falling object has a constant acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² (about 10 m/s²) downward.

A diagram of one object (a dot at its center of mass) with every force exerted on it by other objects drawn as a whole arrow starting on the dot, labeled with its type and agent, lengths in proportion. It never shows velocity, components or a net force arrow.
The number of trips or cycles per second, f = 1/T, in hertz (Hz = 1/s).
A contact force exerted by a surface on an object, along the surface, that opposes the sliding (or the tendency to slide) of the two surfaces against each other.
How one quantity changes when another changes, found from the equation that links them. Written as a factor: "if v doubles, d becomes 4 times as large".
The pressure above atmospheric pressure, P_gauge = P − P₀ = ρgh in a liquid; absolute pressure P includes the atmosphere's P₀ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.
The gravitational force per unit mass at a point, g = F_g/m, in N/kg (the same as m/s²). At a planet's surface g = GM/R²; near Earth it is about 9.8 N/kg and treated as constant.
The attractive force between two objects because of their masses, acting along the line between their centers. Near a planet's surface it is the object's weight, mg.

Mass measured by how strongly an object is pulled by gravity. Experiments find it equal to inertial mass (how strongly the object resists acceleration), which is why all objects fall with the same acceleration (the equivalence principle).
The potential energy of an object-Earth system near Earth's surface: ΔU_g = mgΔy.

terms.term: gravitational potential energy far from a planet
terms.def: The gravitational potential energy of two masses at any separation: U_G = −Gm₁m₂/r, zero at infinite separation.
The contact force a hinge or pivot exerts on an object. Its direction is not fixed in advance; it is whatever balances the other forces, often with both horizontal and vertical parts.
For an ideal spring, F_s = −kΔx: the spring force is proportional to the displacement Δx of its end from the relaxed length, and opposite to it. The spring constant k (N/m) measures stiffness.
The horizontal distance a projectile travels before landing: the horizontal velocity times the time of flight.
terms.topicTitle: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

terms.def: The pressure at a depth h in a fluid at rest: P = P₀ + ρgh, set by depth, not by the container's shape.
A model fluid that is incompressible (constant density) and nonviscous (no internal friction), flowing smoothly; the exam's fluids are ideal unless stated.
A model pulley with no mass and no friction. It changes the direction of an ideal string without changing its tension.
A model spring that has no mass and obeys Hooke's law exactly, so it exerts forces of equal size at its two ends.
A model string that has no mass and does not stretch, so the tension is the same all along it and the objects tied to it move together.
The product of the average force and the time it acts, J = F_avg Δt: a vector in N·s, equal to the area under a force-time graph.
The net impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: J = Δp.
In two-dimensional motion, the horizontal and vertical components each follow their own one-dimensional rules; what happens in one direction does not affect the other. Only the time is shared.
terms.topicTitle: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

terms.def: A collision in which momentum is conserved but the total kinetic energy decreases, the difference becoming thermal energy, sound and deformation.
The tendency of an object to keep its velocity. Mass measures inertia: the more mass, the harder it is to change the velocity. Inertia is not a force.
A reference frame in which Newton's first law holds, such as the ground or a vehicle moving at constant velocity. An accelerating vehicle is a noninertial frame.
The acceleration at one instant: the value the average acceleration approaches as the time interval is made very short.
The velocity at one instant: the value the average velocity approaches as the time interval is made very short.
Two objects acting on each other: pushing, pulling, rubbing or attracting. Every force is one side of an interaction.
A force that one part of a system exerts on another part. Internal forces come in third-law pairs that add to zero for the system.
The parts inside a system and how they are arranged and move relative to each other. When it does not affect the question, the system can be modeled as one object.
y is inversely proportional to x (y ∝ 1/x) when y = k/x: multiplying x by a factor divides y by that factor, so x × y stays constant.
The SI unit of energy: 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s² = 1 N·m.
For circular orbits around the same central body of mass M, T² = (4π²/GM)r³: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit radius.
The three equations for constant acceleration: v = v₀ + at; x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²; v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). Each leaves out one quantity.
The energy an object has because it moves: K = ½mv². A scalar, never negative, that depends on the reference frame.
Friction between surfaces that slide against each other: f_k = μ_k F_N, opposite the direction of sliding.
The angle between a projectile's initial velocity and the horizontal. It sets how the launch speed splits: horizontal v cos θ, vertical v sin θ.
terms.topicTitle: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

terms.def: The perpendicular distance r⊥ from the axis of rotation to a force’s line of action: r⊥ = r sin θ. A force whose line passes through the axis has zero lever arm.
The straight line through a force’s point of application, along the force’s direction, extended both ways.
A relationship whose graph is a straight line, y = mx + b, with slope m and vertical intercept b.
Choosing what to plot so that the graph is a straight line, for example d against t² when d = ½at², so the slope gives the quantity you want.
The size of a vector, with no direction: always zero or positive. The magnitude of a velocity of −4.2 m/s is 4.2 m/s.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: A scalar measure of the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms (kg). The masses of parts add to the mass of the whole.
How an object’s mass is spread out relative to an axis. The same mass placed farther from the axis gives a larger rotational inertia.
The sum of a system's kinetic and potential energies, K + U.
A word in front of a unit that multiplies it by a power of ten: kilo (k) = 10³, centi (c) = 10⁻², milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶.
The product of an object's mass and velocity, p = mv: a vector along the velocity, in kg·m/s.
Bars showing each object's momentum (with its sign) and the system total before and after an interaction; with no net external impulse, the totals match.
A graph of momentum against time; its slope is the net force on the object.
A picture of an object's position at equal time intervals, as dots or images, often with velocity arrows. Growing gaps mean speeding up; shrinking gaps, slowing down.
A torque on a system from an object outside it. Only the net external torque can change a system’s total angular momentum.
The vector sum of all the forces on an object, ΣF. It is found from the free-body diagram and is not itself one of the forces.

The condition in which the buoyant force on an object equals its weight, so it neither rises nor sinks. A fully submerged object is neutrally buoyant when its average density equals the fluid's; a floating object reaches the same balance with only part of it under the surface.
Newton's first law: an object's velocity stays constant (it stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed) unless a nonzero net force acts on it.

terms.term: Newton's first law in rotational form
terms.def: With zero net torque on it, an object’s angular velocity stays constant: at rest stays at rest, turning keeps turning at the same rate.
aka: rotational form of the first law

terms.def: Newton's law of universal gravitation: any two objects attract each other with a force of size |F_g| = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between their centers and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is the gravitational constant.
Newton's second law: the acceleration of an object (or of a system's center of mass) equals the net external force divided by the mass, a = ΣF/m, and points in the direction of the net force.

terms.term: Newton's second law in rotational form
terms.def: α = τ_net/I: an object’s angular acceleration equals the net torque on it divided by its rotational inertia, and turns the way the net torque does.
aka: rotational form of the second law

terms.def: Newton's third law: when object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts a force on A that is equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type. The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other.
Acceleration that changes with time: a curved v-t graph. In this course it is described from graphs and in words, not calculated.
The push of a surface on an object touching it, perpendicular to the surface and away from it (F_N). Its size is whatever the situation requires, not always mg.
The object model: treating an object as a single point that has a position but no size, shape or inner parts. It works when those do not affect the motion described.
I = I_cm + Md²: the rotational inertia about any axis equals the inertia about a parallel axis through the center of mass plus the total mass times the square of the distance between the axes.
The period of a simple pendulum of length ℓ at small angles: T = 2π√(ℓ/g). It does not depend on the bob's mass.
An inelastic collision in which the objects stick together and move with one common velocity, v_f = Σp/Σm.
The time for one complete trip around a circle (or one cycle of a repeating motion), T, in seconds. For uniform circular motion, v = 2πr/T.
In simple harmonic motion the period does not depend on the amplitude: a larger swing is covered at a proportionally larger speed.
The time for one complete cycle of an oscillation, T, in seconds; the frequency is f = 1/T, in hertz.
Motion that repeats itself in equal time intervals, such as a swinging pendulum or a block bouncing on a spring.
Where an object is, measured from an origin along a chosen positive direction, in meters. Along a line it is one signed number, x.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: A graph of position x against time t. Its slope at any instant is the velocity; a straight line means constant velocity, a curve means the velocity changes.
Energy stored in the configuration of a system of objects that interact through conservative forces; it belongs to the system, not to one object.
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done: P = W/Δt, or P = F_∥v at an instant; measured in watts (J/s).
The perpendicular force per unit area on a surface, P = F⊥/A, a scalar measured in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).
An object that, after launch, moves under gravity alone (air resistance negligible): zero horizontal acceleration and a constant downward acceleration g.
terms.topicTitle: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

terms.def: A pulley whose rotational inertia matters. The string’s tensions on its two sides differ, and their difference times the radius gives the torque that spins it up: (F_T1 − F_T2)R = Iα.
The SI unit of angle: the angle for which the distance along a circle equals the radius. One revolution is 2π rad, about 6.28 rad, or 360°.
Solving an equation for one symbol by doing the same operation to both sides, undoing the operations in reverse order.
The point of view from which motion is measured: an observer with a coordinate system that moves with them. A velocity has meaning only relative to some frame.
The velocity of an object as measured in a given frame. Along a line: v(object relative to ground) = v(object relative to frame) + v(frame relative to ground).
A force that points back toward an object's equilibrium position whenever the object is displaced from it.
A triangle with one 90° angle. Its longest side, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse; the Pythagorean theorem says hypotenuse² = leg² + leg².
An object or system that keeps its shape as it moves, so every part of it turns through the same angle in the same time.
Rolling in which the contact point slides, so v_cm ≠ Rω. Kinetic friction then acts and dissipates mechanical energy until the motion matches (or the object stops).
Rolling in which the contact point does not slide on the surface, so the center moves forward one circumference per turn: Δx_cm = RΔθ and v_cm = Rω. Static friction may act but does no work.
The state of an object whose net torque is zero, so its angular velocity does not change. With zero net force as well, an object at rest stays at rest (static equilibrium).
How hard it is to change an object’s rotation about an axis: I = Σmr² for point masses, in kg·m². It depends on the mass and how far that mass is from the axis. Also called moment of inertia.
For constant angular acceleration: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt², and ω² = ω₀² + 2α(θ − θ₀). They mirror the linear equations with θ, ω, α for x, v, a.
The kinetic energy of an object turning about an axis: K = ½Iω², a scalar in joules. An object can have it while its center of mass is at rest.
A quantity with a size (and a unit) but no direction, such as distance, speed, time or mass.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: Writing a number as a value from 1 to 10 times a power of ten, such as 2.5 × 10⁻³ s for 0.0025 s.
One of the agreed units of the International System. Physics 1 uses the base units meter (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass and second (s) for time, and units built from them, such as m/s.
The digits of a measured value that are known, plus one estimated digit. A calculated result keeps as many as the least precise data allow.
Periodic motion caused by a restoring force proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite to it, F = −kx.
A small, heavy bob on a light string swinging under gravity; for small angles its motion is very close to simple harmonic motion.
For an angle θ in a right triangle: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent (SOH CAH TOA).
Motion whose position-time graph is a sine or cosine curve, as in SHM: x = A cos(2πft) or x = A sin(2πft).
The steepness of a line: rise over run, Δy/Δx between two points on the line. Its unit is (y unit)/(x unit), and it tells you the rate at which y changes with x.
How fast an object moves, as a distance per time (m/s): a scalar, the magnitude of the velocity.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: The force a stretched or compressed spring exerts on an object attached to its end, always toward the spring's relaxed length: a stretched spring pulls, a compressed spring pushes.
The period of a block of mass m on a spring of constant k: T = 2π√(m/k). It does not depend on the amplitude or on g.
aka: period of a mass on a spring

terms.def: A dependence on the square of a quantity, y ∝ x²: multiplying x by a factor multiplies y by that factor squared. An inverse square, y ∝ 1/x², divides y by the factor squared.
One of the forms matter takes (solid, liquid or gas), set by how closely its particles are packed and how freely they move.
Friction between surfaces that do not slide against each other. It takes whatever value prevents slipping, up to a maximum of μ_s F_N; usually μ_s is larger than μ_k.
A small label written below a symbol to say which value is meant: x₀ is the starting position, v₁ and v₂ two different velocities.
Putting numbers, with their units, in place of the symbols of an expression, after it has been solved for the unknown.
Everything outside the system you chose. Objects in the surroundings can push or pull on the system.
An answer written with symbols for given quantities instead of numbers, such as t = (x − x₀)/v. The exam asks for these in derivations.
The object or group of objects you choose to study, inside a boundary you draw. Everything else is the surroundings.
The part of an object's acceleration along its velocity, which changes its speed. On a circle it adds to the centripetal part as a vector.
The speed of a point on a turning object, along its circle: v = rω, with ω in rad/s. Points farther from the axis move faster.
The pull of a rope, string or cable on an object attached to it, directed along the rope away from the object (F_T).
Mechanical energy turned into thermal energy (and sound) by nonconservative forces such as kinetic friction; it is still energy, just no longer mechanical.
The time between two moments: Δt = t(final) − t(initial), in seconds.
How long a projectile is in the air. It is set by the vertical motion alone: the vertical launch velocity, the height and g.
terms.topicTitle: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

terms.def: Adding vectors by drawing each one starting at the tip of the one before; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip. In practice, add the x-components and the y-components separately.
The turning effect of a force about an axis: τ = r⊥F = rF sin θ, in N·m. Sign gives the direction, clockwise or counterclockwise. The net torque is the sum with signs.
A graph of torque against the angle turned. The area under it is the work done by the torque.
The speed of fluid leaving a small opening a depth h below an open surface: v = √(2gh), derived from Bernoulli's equation.

The total mechanical energy of a satellite and the body it orbits, E = K + U with U_G = −GMm/r (zero at infinite separation). It is negative for a bound orbit; for a circular orbit E = −K = −GMm/(2r).
The state of an object whose net force is zero (ΣF = 0, in every direction). Its velocity stays constant, which includes staying at rest.
The kinetic energy of a rolling object: K = ½Mv_cm² + ½Iω², the translational kinetic energy of its center of mass plus its rotational kinetic energy about the center.
aka: total kinetic energy of a rolling object

terms.def: Motion in a circle at a constant speed. The velocity changes direction continuously, so the object accelerates toward the center.
Changing a value to another unit by multiplying by a fraction equal to 1, such as (1 m / 100 cm), so the old unit cancels.
A letter that stands for a physical quantity, such as x for position, v for velocity or t for time. It stands for a number with a unit.
A quantity with both a size and a direction, such as displacement or velocity. Along a line, its sign gives its direction.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: The parts of a vector along perpendicular axes: for magnitude A at angle θ from the x-axis, the x-component is A cos θ and the y-component is A sin θ. The vector is the sum of its components.
Adding vectors along one line by adding their signed values: +12 m and −5 m add to +7 m. The result is the resultant.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.def: How fast an object moves and in which direction: displacement per time, in m/s. A vector; its magnitude is the speed.
terms.topicTitle: Scalars and Vectors on a Line

terms.term: velocity of the center of mass
terms.def: The velocity of a system's center of mass: the system's momentum divided by its total mass, v_cm = Σp/Σm.
A graph of velocity v against time t. Its slope is the acceleration and the area between it and the time axis is the displacement.

A circle in a vertical plane, such as a loop-the-loop. At the top, gravity and the track's normal force both point to the center; the minimum speed there is when gravity alone supplies the net force, v = √(gr).
The volume of fluid passing a point each second, Av (area × speed), in m³/s.

The pull of Earth (or another planet) on an object, F_g = mg, pointing down toward the planet's center. Near Earth, g = 9.8 m/s² (10 m/s² is accepted). Mass stays the same everywhere; weight depends on where you are.
Energy moved into or out of a system by a force acting along a displacement: W = F d cos θ, a scalar in joules that can be positive, negative or zero.
The work done on a turning object by a torque: W = τΔθ for a constant torque, with Δθ in radians. Positive when the torque is in the direction of turning.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK.
The configuration chosen to have zero potential energy; any choice works because only changes in potential energy matter.
